posts.title: Loose boards over a stairwell are not a cover — they are a missing temporary works item
posts.excerpt: HSE press release 21 September 2026: Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd was fined £300,000 plus £9,284.05 costs at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026 after Joseph Tuck, 24, fell one storey through an unprotected stairwell opening on a four-dwelling site in January 2024. Loose scaffold boards that had previously covered the opening had been removed. There was no edge protection and no alternative sub-floor access. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and HART rescued him unconscious. He sustained serious spinal injuries and has not returned to a physical job. Floor openings are temporary works.
posts.linkedinReady:
A stairwell waiting for a flight is not an empty hole. It is a temporary works opening with a one-storey drop onto concrete.

HSE published the outcome on 21 September 2026. Joseph Tuck, 24, a father of one and a temporary scaffolding labourer in his second week, stepped backwards through an unprotected stairwell on a four-house site being built by Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd in January 2024. Loose scaffold boards that had sat over the opening had been removed. There was no edge protection. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and HART recovered him unconscious. He suffered serious spinal injuries and has not returned to a physical job.

The housebuilder was found guilty on three charges for failing to plan and supervise work at height and to prevent a fall. Fine: £300,000 plus £9,284.05 costs at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026. HSE’s release does not allege an offence by the scaffolding employer.

Register the opening. Fit a secured cover or designed edge protection before anyone works next to it. Loose boards that can be lifted are not a cover.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #WorkAtHeight #HSE #EdgeProtection #BS5975

body.p: The Health and Safety Executive published a prosecution release on 21 September 2026. Joseph Tuck, 24, a father of one, was working as a temporary labourer for a scaffolding company in January 2024 on a site of four new domestic dwellings being constructed by Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd. It was his second week on the job. He stepped backwards through an opening intended for a staircase that had not yet been installed and fell one storey onto a concrete floor. The stairwell opening had not been securely covered — previous loose scaffold boards had been removed — and the open edges were not protected. There were no alternative means of accessing the sub-floor. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and the HART team rescued Mr Tuck, who had fallen unconscious. He sustained serious spinal injuries, was unable to work for months, and has not returned to a physical job. Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd, formerly of 1 Bretton Place, Otley Road, Guiseley, Leeds LS20 8FL, was found guilty on three charges: it failed to properly plan and appropriately supervise work at height and to take suitable and sufficient measures to prevent a fall. The company was fined £300,000 and ordered to pay £9,284.05 in costs at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026. HSE Inspector Louise Redgrove said falls from height remain one of the leading causes of death in construction, accounting for around a quarter of all fatal injuries to workers each year, and that this was a wholly avoidable incident caused by basic failures in planning and supervision.

A stairwell, lift shaft, service riser or floor void before the permanent flight, slab or cover is in place is a temporary works item. The hazard is a fall through an opening, not only a fall from an external edge. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require suitable and sufficient measures to prevent a fall, including where there is a risk of falling through openings in floors, roofs or work platforms. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure that puts openings, edge protection, crash decks and scaffold interfaces on the temporary works register, names a Temporary Works Coordinator and Temporary Works Supervisor, and requires a design or standard solution, inspection and a permit before people work next to the void. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A domestic house plot can become high risk where boards are loose, covers are removed for access and not reinstated, there is no alternative route, and the person nearest the opening is new to site. The HSE release was brought against the housebuilder. Scaffold contractors still need their own interface control: do not leave a void because the housebuilder owns the hole.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every stairwell, lift shaft, riser and floor opening as a temporary works item from first slab pour until the permanent flight or cover is fixed.
Specify a secured cover (fixed, marked, load-rated, not loose boards) or designed edge protection. Loose scaffold boards that can be lifted for access are not a cover.
If the cover must be removed for a task, treat removal as a controlled change: exclusion zone, alternative protection, named person, and reinstatement before the next trade walks the floor.
Plan access to the sub-floor. HSE recorded that there were no alternative means of accessing the sub-floor on this site — that is a planning failure, not a rescue problem.
Interface the scaffold contractor, housebuilder and follow-on trades on the same opening. The person who removes the boards is responsible for the void they leave.
Inspect openings at the start of each shift and after any board movement. Record the inspection. A missing cover is a stop.
Provisional design or check category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Public, multi-storey or occupied-building openings escalate.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: Do not copy CIRIA C761 shear enhancement onto the tension side of a piled crane base
posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1552 (29 June 2026) flags Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761 Tower crane foundation and tie design. The example applies shear enhancement on the compression side of a square piled base. The Expert Panel generally agrees that enhancement cannot be used where both the crane leg and the pile are in tension, because no compression strut can form. Copying the spreadsheet or the example without checking the tension-side shear planes can leave a safety-critical temporary works foundation over-utilised. Design for full shear demand, or use a strut-and-tie model, and treat the base as a Cat 2/3 item under the project procedure.
posts.linkedinReady:
A tower crane base is a single, safety-critical temporary works element. Copying a worked example is not a design.

CROSS-UK Report 1552 (29 June 2026) reviews Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761. The example checks beam shear on the compression side of a square piled base and applies shear enhancement where the load is close to the pile. The Reporter asked what happens on the opposite side, where overturning puts both the crane leg and the pile into tension. The Expert Panel generally agrees: no compression strut, so no shear enhancement for the uplift case. Design for the full shear demand, or run a strut-and-tie model. The Panel also warns that spreadsheet copies of guidance examples are replacing judgement.

For contractors: register the crane base, issue a design brief that includes in-service and out-of-service wind, climbing and chocking, and get an independent check. Do not treat C761 as a permitted standard solution. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC.

#TemporaryWorks #TowerCranes #CROSSUK #CIRIAC761 #BS5975

body.p: CROSS-UK published Safety Report 1552 on 29 June 2026. A Reporter reviewed Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761 Tower crane foundation and tie design, which covers a square piled tower crane base. The example designs the base as a beam in each direction for bending, beam shear and punching shear, and identifies diagonal overturning as controlling beam shear for the example geometry. Shear planes are checked adjacent to the crane leg and adjacent to the pile on the compression side. Because those planes sit within two times the effective depth of the pile, the example applies shear enhancement — the increase in capacity when a near-support load is carried partly by a diagonal compression strut — and concludes capacity is adequate. The Reporter noted that the corresponding planes on the tension side, where overturning puts the crane leg and pile into tension, are not checked. The guide treats tension-side shear as less onerous by inspection. The Reporter’s own calculations indicated that tension-side shear adjacent to the pile could be substantially over-utilised if enhancement is removed.

The CROSS Expert Panel thanked the Reporter and generally agreed with the core point: shear enhancement cannot be applied in the worked example when both the crane leg and the pile are in tension, because no compression strut can form between those locations on the reinforcement shown. Designers should not rely on enhancement for the uplift condition. A simplified approach is to design the base for the full shear demand without enhancement, accepting a deeper slab or more reinforcement in exchange for fewer detailing errors and a more buildable cage. A strut-and-tie analysis is an alternative. The Panel also noted that the example’s assumption that the applied load acts close to the pile may not align with other parts of C761, PD 6687-2 or BS EN 1992-1-1, and pointed to the IStructE pile-cap technical guidance note and Design of Transfer Slabs. It warned that crane-base design is becoming standardised through spreadsheets copied from worked examples, which can hide project-specific load paths. CROSS recommends the report is brought to everyone who designs or builds piled crane bases and that CIRIA considers clarification of Worked Example 3, including cranked and tied cranes, climbing frames and chocking.

A tower crane foundation is temporary works. Collapse or excessive rotation of the base is a high-consequence event for the crane, the load, the public and the permanent structure. CIRIA C761 is industry good practice, not a permitted standard solution and not a substitute for project-specific design and check. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure that puts the base on the temporary works register, names a Temporary Works Coordinator and requires a design brief, independent check and permit before the crane is erected or climbed. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A square piled cap taken from a guidance example can become high risk where overturning produces tension piles, where the geometry differs from the example, where climbing or chocking changes the load path, or where the checker only repeats the spreadsheet. The TWC’s job is to stop that copy-and-paste reaching site.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every tower crane base, rail, tie and climbing frame as a temporary works item before the first pour or the first chock.

Issue a design brief that states crane type, in-service and out-of-service wind, climbing stages, chocking, tie levels, pile layout, GI and adjacent structures. Do not accept a C761 example printout as the brief.

Require the designer to show shear checks on both the compression and tension sides of the base under overturning. If shear enhancement is used, the designer must demonstrate a compression strut can form.
Where enhancement is uncertain, instruct design for full shear demand or a strut-and-tie model. Record the choice on the design certificate.
Provisional design and check category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Piled crane bases are typically independent Cat 2 or Cat 3, not Cat 0.
Hold points: GI accepted, pile as-built versus design, cage inspection before pour, concrete strength before erection, permit-to-erect, permit-to-climb, inspection after each climb or storm.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

Subject to project-specific verification of crane data, wind, ground, pile layout, base geometry, climbing and chocking, and to acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. posts.title: Unsupported trench, spoil at the edge, and a contracts manager who walked past it
posts.excerpt: HSE press release 9 September 2026: after a trial at the Old Bailey, T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 plus £40,000 costs and Appledorn Developments Limited £500,000. Gheorghita Arsene, 33, died on 24 June 2020 at Park Road, Banstead, when unsupported trench walls buried him under about two tonnes of soil while he replaced a damaged pipe. Spoil sat immediately next to the edge. Contracts manager Anthony O’Connor had seen another worker in the same unsupported excavation that day. He received a 10-month sentence, suspended for 18 months, and 150 hours unpaid work. Pipe repairs in a deep trench are temporary works, not a quick dig.
posts.linkedinReady:
An unsupported trench with spoil stacked at the lip is not a small civils job. It is a temporary works item with a known collapse mechanism.

HSE published the Old Bailey outcome on 9 September 2026. Gheorghita Arsene, 33, died on 24 June 2020 at Park Road, Banstead, while replacing a damaged pipe at the bottom of a deep trench dug with a three-tonne excavator. The walls had no support. Spoil sat immediately next to the edge. About two tonnes of soil buried him. He died at the scene.

T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 plus £40,000 costs. Principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited was fined £500,000. Both were convicted under Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Self-employed contracts manager Anthony O’Connor had seen another worker in the same unsupported excavation that day. He pleaded guilty under Section 7, received 10 months’ imprisonment suspended for 18 months, and 150 hours unpaid work.

Register the excavation. Design the support. Keep spoil and plant outside the influence zone. Inspect before anyone enters. A manager who sees an unsupported trench and walks on is part of the failure.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #Excavations #HSE #BS5975 #TrenchSafety

body.p: The Health and Safety Executive published a prosecution release on 9 September 2026. Gheorghita Arsene, 33, known as Geo, was working at Park Road, Banstead, Surrey on 24 June 2020, replacing a damaged pipe at the bottom of a deep trench that had been excavated with a three-tonne digger. He was clearing soil with a shovel and pickaxe when the trench walls collapsed without warning. Rescue was attempted. He was buried under approximately two tonnes of soil and died at the scene. Following a trial at the Old Bailey on 9 September 2026, principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited and subcontractor T Vaughan Limited were convicted of breaching Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 and ordered to pay costs of £40,000. Appledorn Developments Limited was fined £500,000. Anthony O’Connor, a self-employed contracts manager working for T Vaughan Limited, pleaded guilty on 22 May 2026 to breaching Section 7 of the same Act. He was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, and ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work. The prosecution was brought by the Crown Prosecution Service after a five-year joint investigation by Surrey Police and HSE.

The joint investigation found there were no supports in the trench and excavated soil had been deposited immediately next to it. Earlier that day Anthony O’Connor had observed another worker in the same unsupported excavation. HSE stated he was aware of the measures required to prevent a trench collapse and failed to ensure they were in place. An HSE spokesperson said Mr Arsene’s death was as horrifying as it was preventable, and that he lost his life because basic precautions were not in place to protect workers from the well-known risks of excavation work.

Pipe replacement at the base of a deep excavation is a temporary works activity. Collapse of unsupported faces, surcharge from spoil heaps, plant at the edge and people working in the base are the classic load path. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase so that work is carried out without risks to health and safety, so far as is reasonably practicable. Excavation support is an engineered control: trench box, shoring, batter or other designed system, selected against ground, groundwater, depth, surcharge and duration. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure that puts the excavation on the temporary works register, names a Temporary Works Coordinator and Temporary Works Supervisor, and requires a design brief, inspection and permit before entry. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A short utility trench can become high risk where the face is vertical, spoil is at the lip, there is no GI, and people are working in the base. Individual duty holders who see an unprotected excavation and do not stop the work are part of the control failure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every trench and excavation as a temporary works item before digging starts. Depth, ground, groundwater, adjacent structures, services and spoil locations belong on the brief.
Do not permit entry to an unsupported excavation. Support, batter or a proprietary box must be designed or selected, installed as specified, and inspected before first entry and after any change.
Keep spoil, plant and materials outside the influence zone of the face. Spoil stacked at the lip is a surcharge load, not storage.
Confirm services, CAT and permit-to-dig before the bucket goes in. A damaged pipe at the base is often why the trench exists — treat buried services as a live interface.
Name the TWC and TWS. A contracts manager who sees someone in an unsupported trench has a duty to stop the work, not to note it and walk on.
RAMS and ITP must name the support system, inspection frequency, hold points for permit-to-enter, and the rescue plan. A generic excavation paragraph is not a method.
Provisional design or check category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Deep, close-to-structure, wet or public-interface trenches escalate.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.
